findings.title: Pass-the-Hash attack — Event ID 4624+4648+4672 cluster
findings.firstness: Windows Security.evtx contains 178 findings across 146 event chains and 5908 total events. The EventLogCorrelator flags HIGH_SEVERITY_25 (process creation without SafeMode), HIGH_SEVERITY_7045 (new service installed), and PASS_THE_HASH (4624+4648+4672 co-occurrence cluster). Composite score=19/20. 33 temporal gaps detected.
findings.secondness: The PASS_THE_HASH pattern requires the simultaneous presence of three distinct event IDs: 4624 (logon with NtLmSsp authentication), 4648 (explicit credentials used), and 4672 (special privileges assigned to new logon). This co-occurrence within the same temporal window is not produced by normal interactive user logons, service accounts, or automated scheduled tasks. The HIGH_SEVERITY_7045 signal (new service installation) in the same timeline multiplies the structural improbability: legitimate maintenance windows would not coincide with credential relay patterns.
findings.thirdness: The actor used a credential relay technique — injecting a captured NTLM hash to authenticate as another user without knowing the plaintext password. This is a deliberate lateral movement technique (PtH) requiring specialized tooling (Mimikatz, Invoke-TheHash, Impacket psexec). The 7045 co-occurrence suggests the relay was used to install a service for persistence. Carnegie pattern: impersonation — borrowing a legitimated user's identity to bypass authorization boundaries that block the attacker's own account.
findings.carnegie: Impersonation — credential relay weaponizes Windows NTLM trust model to borrow a legitimate identity
mitre: T1550.002 — Use Alternate Authentication Material: Pass the Hash
T1543.003 — Create or Modify System Process: Windows Service (co-incident 7045)
findings.devil_advocate: Windows Event ID 4624 (type 3 — network logon with NTLM) is routinely produced by file share access, printer access, and any network authentication in a domain that falls back to NTLM (e.g., when Kerberos is unavailable because the target is referenced by IP address rather than hostname). Event 4672 fires for any account with special privilege groups including built-in local administrators performing routine tasks. Event 4648 fires for runas and for scheduled tasks using stored credentials. A high-volume Windows system could produce these three events in proximity by coincidence. STRENGTH: MEDIUM. REBUTTAL: The EventLogCorrelator's PASS_THE_HASH detection requires the co-occurrence within the same logon chain (matching Logon ID across events), not mere temporal proximity. This is a correlated cluster, not independent event coincidence. Additionally, the z=3.04 signal (99.9th percentile) indicates the cluster density exceeds normal operational baseline by a statistically significant margin.
findings.corroboration: F-004 (SYSTEM hive service persistence, REGISTRY_RTR z=1.960) — service installation (7045) is mechanistically linked to registry service keys. Two independent artifact classes (EVTX + Registry hive) both show service-related anomalies. Daubert corroboration gate: PASSED.
findings.daubert_gate: Two independent artifact classes (Security.evtx + SYSTEM registry hive). INTENT threshold met.

findings.title: RUNDLL32.EXE proxy execution — 5 prefetch records, repeated invocations
findings.pipeline_signal: PREFETCH_ANALYZER z=1.750 confidence=0.73 — suspicious_count=12, suspicious_executables=[RUNDLL32.EXE x5]
findings.firstness: Prefetch directory contains 225 .pf files (3 unparsed). PrefetchAnalyzer identifies 12 suspicious_execution records. Of the parseable ANTI_FORENSIC_PREFETCH_SIGNS matches, RUNDLL32.EXE appears 5 times — indicating multiple distinct invocations with different DLL arguments (Windows creates a separate .pf per unique command-line hash). Total prefetch count=225 is within the normal Windows operational range (50-300); no PREFETCH_WIPE anti-forensic deletion pattern detected.
findings.secondness: RUNDLL32.EXE has a documented dual-use profile: it is a legitimate Windows shell for loading COM in-process servers, but it is also the second most abused LOLBin for proxy execution (T1218.011). Multiple distinct prefetch entries (unique command-line hash per .pf) indicate repeated use with different payloads or targets, not a single legitimate software installation routine. Legitimate software installers that use RUNDLL32 produce 1-2 prefetch entries. 5 distinct entries suggest operational use.
findings.thirdness: Proxy execution via RUNDLL32.EXE bypasses application whitelisting controls and process reputation systems by inheriting the trust of a signed Windows binary. An attacker using this technique is specifically exploiting the fact that rundll32.exe appears in every Windows security exception list. Carnegie: authority transfer — borrowing Microsoft's signing certificate to legitimize attacker-controlled DLL code.
findings.carnegie: Authority transfer — LOLBin proxy execution borrows Microsoft signing certificate trust
mitre: T1218.011 — System Binary Proxy Execution: Rundll32
findings.devil_advocate: RUNDLL32.EXE is a standard Windows system binary used by countless legitimate applications including Windows itself (Control Panel applets, screensavers, OLE/COM registration, Windows Update hooks). 5 prefetch entries for RUNDLL32.EXE is low for an active Windows workstation — most production systems would show 10-20+. The prefetch count alone cannot distinguish legitimate from malicious invocations because the content of the DLL arguments is not available from prefetch files alone. STRENGTH: HIGH. REBUTTAL: The elevated count is suspicious in context (co-occurrence with PASS_THE_HASH in the same system), but standalone this finding cannot be rated INTENT. SUSPICION is the accurate rating.
findings.corroboration: F-001 (PtH attack on same system). PREFETCH_ANALYZER and EVENT_LOG are independent artifact classes, but the prefetch finding alone does not independently confirm proxy execution intent — it only confirms RUNDLL32 was run. SUSPICION is the correct ceiling.
findings.daubert_gate: Single artifact class (prefetch only). DLL argument content unavailable from .pf files. SUSPICION cap applied.

findings.title: Instant messaging client (PIDGIN) — potential exfiltration vector
findings.pipeline_signal: PREFETCH_ANALYZER suspicious_count=12 (PIDGIN.EXE not in ANTI_FORENSIC_PREFETCH_SIGNS — separate coverage gap noted)
findings.firstness: Prefetch directory execution evidence includes PIDGIN.EXE, an open-source multi-protocol instant messaging client supporting IRC, XMPP, AIM, and other protocols. PIDGIN is not in the current ANTI_FORENSIC_PREFETCH_SIGNS blacklist (this is a documented coverage gap, separate from the L-043 serialization bug).
findings.secondness: PIDGIN is an uncommon enterprise application — corporate environments typically prohibit or block non-standard IM clients in favor of approved tools (Teams, Zoom, Slack). Its presence on what appears to be a domain-joined Windows system is anomalous. IM clients have been documented as C2 exfiltration channels (XMPP over port 5222, easily confused with standard web traffic).
findings.thirdness: If used as an exfiltration vector, PIDGIN would operate over a persistent encrypted channel that blends with standard HTTPS/SSL traffic, making detection by network DLP difficult. This is consistent with the LOLBin and IM exfiltration pattern documented in red team tradecraft. However, this is a hypothesis, not a confirmed finding.
findings.carnegie: Institutional trust exploitation (potential) — IM traffic blends with legitimate web protocol traffic
mitre: T1048.003 — Exfiltration Over Alternative Protocol: Exfiltration Over Unencrypted Non-C2 Protocol (candidate)
findings.devil_advocate: PIDGIN is free, legitimate software installed by millions of users for personal IM use. Many organizations allow personal devices or bring-your-own-device policies that would permit PIDGIN. A user could have installed it for IRC tech support channels, open source project communication, or personal use unrelated to any attacker activity. Without PIDGIN log files or network capture showing anomalous IM traffic, this is speculative. STRENGTH: HIGH. REBUTTAL: Acknowledged. SUSPICION LOW is appropriate. INFERRED status requires corroboration not present in this evidence set.
findings.corroboration: No independent artifact confirms PIDGIN was used for exfiltration. PIDGIN .log files not in evidence copy. Network capture not available. INFERRED — corroboration required.
findings.daubert_gate: No second independent source. SUSPICION LOW — INFERRED status. Cannot be upgraded without network artifacts or PIDGIN log files.

findings.title: Registry service persistence — SYSTEM hive, 77 persistence keys
findings.pipeline_signal: REGISTRY_RTR z=1.960 confidence=0.755 — persistence_count=77 in SYSTEM hive (hive_sha256 dabf4453...)
findings.firstness: Five registry hives analyzed. Four show persistence_count=0 (NTUSER.DAT, SAM, and two other hives). The SYSTEM hive (dabf4453...) shows persistence_count=77. No timestomp anomalies detected. No USB artifacts. No usb_count anomalies.
findings.secondness: A persistence_count of 77 in SYSTEM\CurrentControlSet\Services is elevated for a workstation. While SYSTEM hives on production Windows workstations commonly accumulate 40-80 service entries over time (OS services, AV, drivers, enterprise agents), the co-occurrence with Event ID 7045 (new service installed, F-001) indicates at least one of these 77 entries was created during the investigation period rather than pre-existing.
findings.thirdness: Service persistence (T1543.003) is a standard post-exploitation persistence mechanism: an attacker who has achieved SYSTEM privileges (via PtH or privilege escalation) installs a Windows service that survives reboots and runs under SYSTEM authority. The service key in HKLM\SYSTEM\CurrentControlSet\Services is written once and persists silently — no user interaction required after installation.
findings.carnegie: None detected at the persistence technique level. Stealth through normalcy — 77 services is within normal range, making the malicious entry hard to identify without differential analysis.
mitre: T1543.003 — Create or Modify System Process: Windows Service
findings.devil_advocate: 77 service keys in SYSTEM hive is within normal range for an enterprise Windows workstation with standard software (AV, endpoint agent, printer drivers, network adapter drivers). Event 7045 fires for any new service including Windows Update driver installations, hardware plug-and-play events, and legitimate software installs. Without identifying the specific service name that corresponds to 7045 in the event log, we cannot determine whether the 77-entry persistence_count represents attacker activity or normal system administration. STRENGTH: HIGH. REBUTTAL: Acknowledged. Confirmed by two independent sources (SYSTEM hive + Security.evtx 7045) but specific malicious service not isolated. SUSPICION MEDIUM is the accurate rating.
findings.corroboration: F-001 Security.evtx Event ID 7045 (new service installed) is mechanistically linked to registry SYSTEM hive service key creation. Two independent artifact classes confirm service installation occurred. SUSPICION MEDIUM — cannot upgrade to INTENT without isolating the specific service key created by the attacker.
findings.daubert_gate: Two independent sources (EVTX + Registry hive). However, specific attacker service key not isolated from 77 total keys. SUSPICION MEDIUM — Daubert corroboration gate requires specific key attribution for INTENT.

findings.title: Browser suspicious downloads — 4 flagged of 24 total
findings.pipeline_signal: BROWSER_FORENSICS z=1.625 confidence=0.71 — SUSPICIOUS_DOWNLOAD, 4/24 downloads flagged, 463 URLs
findings.firstness: Chromium browser History shows 24 total downloads and 463 URLs. BrowserForensics flags 4 downloads as SUSPICIOUS_DOWNLOAD. No C2 count detected.
findings.secondness: 4 out of 24 downloads (16.7%) flagged as suspicious. The browser profile shows active use (463 URLs). Without the specific download URLs or filenames, the 16.7% suspicious rate is a weak signal.
findings.thirdness: Suspicious browser downloads could indicate tool staging — downloading attacker tools via browser to blend with normal web traffic. However, this is a very weak signal without URL/filename context.
findings.devil_advocate: SUSPICIOUS_DOWNLOAD detection in BrowserForensics is a heuristic based on download extension and source domain, not confirmed malware. 4 flagged downloads from 463 URLs is a 0.86% rate across all browsing activity. Users routinely download tools, scripts, and executables for legitimate purposes. Without confirming the specific downloaded files or their hashes against known malware databases, this is statistical noise. STRENGTH: HIGH. REBUTTAL: Acknowledged. SUSPICION LOW maintained. FALSE_SECONDNESS self-correction applied — scenario-name bias removed from assessment.
findings.self_correction: FALSE_SECONDNESS applied by validate_and_correct_analysis: initial SUSPICION MEDIUM rating was inflated by implicit scenario-context bias (OWL case name associated with known attacker tooling). After removing scenario context, purely technical evidence supports only SUSPICION LOW.
findings.corroboration: No second independent source confirming downloaded content is attacker tooling. INFERRED.
findings.daubert_gate: Single artifact class. SUSPICION LOW — INFERRED.

verdict_rationale: EVENT_LOG z=3.04 (99.9th percentile) anchors verdict. PASS_THE_HASH co-occurrence cluster (4624+4648+4672) confirmed by EventLogCorrelator across 5908 events. REGISTRY_RTR z=1.960 provides independent corroboration via SYSTEM hive service persistence mechanistically linked to Security.evtx Event 7045. Two independent artifact classes confirm lateral movement and persistence. CAIE composite=0.1018 (NOISE) is expected and architecturally correct: log_entry evidence type carries spoofability=0.85 penalty by design; CAIE is not the verdict authority for log-only evidence. Trust fusion composite=1.0 confirms artifact integrity. Not MALICE: no active anti-forensic concealment detected (prefetch count=225 normal, no log deletion, no timestomping).
